quotes.quote: The estimator is the rule count divided by sample size. Sixteen percent is the estimate realized by this sample. In the article’s flagged-signup example, the same denominator estimates abuse among flags: review precision, not recall or the false-positive rate.

answers.reason: The sample comes from flagged signups, so 30/150 = 20% estimates abuse among flags, or review precision.

quotes.quote: Four times the independent labels roughly halves the standard error, the typical movement of the estimate.
Bootstrap draws reuse those IDs with replacement.
Extra repetitions refine the calculation while the original evidence stays at a hundred labels.

answers.reason: Both fractions are 20%, and 600 is four times 150, so the larger sample has roughly half the standard error. Bootstrap repetitions reuse existing evidence.

quotes.quote: Wald uses a zero estimated standard error and collapses there. Wilson still accepts rates above zero: ten clean labels leave uncertainty.
For zero positives among n independent labels, the two-sided ninety-five-percent Wilson upper bound is one point nine six squared divided by the sum of n and one point nine six squared.
With ten observed zeros, every resample is all zeros. Its percentile interval collapses. Resampling can only recombine observed outcomes.

answers.reason: Substituting n = 20 gives 1.96²/(20 + 1.96²) ≈ 16.1%. Collapsed Wald and bootstrap intervals do not establish a zero population rate.

quotes.quote: Use the known mix to rebuild the whole. Per thousand messages, routine questions contribute eighty-four expected specialist cases. Billing adds fifty; account access adds forty-two. Join those contributions: one hundred seventy-six per thousand, or seventeen point six percent.
Sample across the target queue, or weight separately sampled slice rates by their population shares.

answers.reason: The weighted rate is 0.50×0.10 + 0.30×0.20 + 0.20×0.40 = 0.19, or 19%. The first slice alone targets its own 10% rate.

quotes.quote: It crosses our twenty-percent staffing threshold, so this sample supports rates on either side. Our original choice still needs evidence.
The report still carries the counts, interval, selection plan, and independently reviewed labels.

answers.reason: The interval [13.0%, 29.4%] includes rates below and above 25%, so the minimum-quality threshold remains unresolved. Report the counts, interval and selection.

quotes.quote: A preselected model-score bucket forecasts twenty percent and yields sixteen positives among a hundred new labels. Place that forecast against its Wilson interval. Twenty percent is compatible here; further held-out evidence can resolve a smaller gap.
Calibration uses a separate preselected score bucket and held-out labels. One compatible interval does not establish calibration of the whole model.

answers.reason: The forecast of 25% lies within [11.8%, 31.8%], so it is compatible with this bucket’s labels. This single comparison does not establish whole-model calibration.

quotes.quote: The estimator is the rule count divided by sample size.
For our Beta two-two prior, use that peak. Add one success term and one failure term to this calculation. The mode becomes two sevenths.
Our maximum-likelihood fraction is sixteen percent; this MAP mode is about sixteen point seven. Fixed prior strength has less influence as the observed counts grow.

answers.reason: Both MLEs equal 0.25. Adding one success and one failure gives MAP modes (2+1)/(8+2) = 3/10 and (50+1)/(200+2) = 51/202. The smaller sample shifts more.

quotes.quote: Ninety-five percent is the method's approximate coverage target across repetitions. Exact coverage varies with rate and sample size. This confidence interval concerns the population rate. A prediction range for a future sample fraction needs a separate calculation because that new sample has its own variation.

answers.reason: Confidence coverage concerns the population rate across repeated intervals. The next 50-label fraction has additional sampling variation and needs a separate prediction calculation.

quotes.quote: Keep the labeling rubric fixed and resolve ambiguous cases independently of model output. Have two reviewers label the same cases separately, without scores or each other's answers, and measure their agreement before resolving disagreements. A narrower interval cannot repair labels that were changed to match the prediction.

answers.reason: A fixed rubric, review blinded to scores, and independent agreement checks address compromised labels. Narrower intervals or more bootstrap repetitions cannot repair them.
